N4.label: N4 / L1 – Landlord says rent is owed
board_decides: Was the N4 notice valid, and did you pay everything owing before its termination date? Paying in full by that date voids the notice.
How much is owed, including rent that came due after the application was filed.
Under section 83, whether it would be unfair to evict you: refuse the eviction, delay it, or make it conditional on a payment plan.

items.label: Proof of every payment you made
items.why: The Board works out the arrears from both sides' records. E-transfer confirmations, receipts and bank statements let you challenge the landlord's ledger.

items.label: Proof of income and expenses, if you will ask for a payment plan
items.why: Members often refuse a payment plan when the tenant has no documents showing it is affordable. Pay stubs, benefit statements and a simple monthly budget make the plan believable.
documents: Pay stubs or an employment letter
ODSP / Ontario Works / CPP / EI statements
A monthly budget (Housekeeper can build one)

items.label: Your household circumstances (section 83)
items.why: Children, disability or health issues, benefits income, how long you have lived there, and how hard it is to find another home can lead the Board to delay or refuse an eviction. Documents make these facts easier to accept.

examples.excerpt: RR testified the source of income for his household is the $2,103.00 he receives monthly from ODSP.
Relief from Eviction 10. The Tenant receives monthly benefits from the Ontario Disability Support Program (ODSP) who pays a portion of the rent, approximately $500.00, directly to the Landlord.

items.label: Repair problems you want to raise (section 82) – give notice in writing first
items.why: In a rent arrears hearing you can raise the landlord's maintenance failures, but only if you gave the landlord and the LTB a written description of each issue and copies of your evidence before the hearing. The Notice of Hearing package says at least 7 days before. Without that, members often refuse to hear the issues.
documents: Written description of each issue (Housekeeper can draft it)
Your written repair requests to the landlord
Proof you sent the disclosure, with the date

items.label: If the landlord is in serious breach (section 83(3)(a)): corroborating evidence
items.why: If the landlord is in serious breach of their obligations, the Board must refuse the eviction. Members want evidence beyond your own testimony: photos, technician or inspection reports, utility records, and messages to the landlord.
documents: Municipal property standards or inspection reports

examples.excerpt: The Tenant now seeks to engage section 83(3)(a) of the Act, requiring the Board (if satisfied that the Landlord is in serious breach) to mandatorily deny eviction.
Section 83(3)(a) of the Act states that where a Landlord is in serious breach of their responsibilities of the Act, the Board must mandatorily refuse eviction.

items.label: Attend the hearing, and speak to Tenant Duty Counsel first
items.why: If you do not attend, the hearing goes ahead on the landlord's evidence alone. Tenant Duty Counsel gives free legal advice to tenants on the day of the hearing.

examples.excerpt: Prior to mediation, the Tenant did not utilize the services of Tenant Duty Counsel. The parties agreed that: 1. As of the hearing date, the Tenant was still in possession of the rental unit. 2.
The Tenant also consulted with Tenant Duty Counsel prior to the mediation. The parties mutually agreed to resolve all matters at issue in the application and requested an order on consent.

N5.label: N5 / L2 – Landlord alleges interference or damage
board_decides: Did the conduct described in the N5 happen, and was it serious enough?
For a first N5: did you void it by stopping the conduct (or paying for or repairing the damage) within 7 days?
Under section 83, whether eviction would be unfair in your circumstances.

items.label: Your account of each incident in the N5
items.why: The landlord must prove the conduct. A dated account of each incident, with messages or witness names, lets you dispute what did not happen.
documents: A dated timeline of each incident
Messages with the landlord or neighbours
Names of witnesses who can attend

examples.excerpt: The Landlord's agent testified that the Tenants did not void the N5 notice.

Because the Landlords did not give any evidence that the N5 notice was not voided and consequently the Member found that the N5 notice was voided, any evidence about these disturbances would have been

items.tab_name: Proof the Conduct Stopped / Damage Repaired
items.label: Proof you stopped the conduct or fixed the damage in time
items.why: A first N5 is void if the tenant stops the conduct, or pays for or repairs the damage, within 7 days.
documents: Messages to the landlord confirming the issue stopped

items.label: Your household circumstances (section 83)
items.why: The Board considers whether evicting you would be unfair, for example because of children, disability or how long you have lived there.

N12.label: N12 / L2 – Landlord or family wants to move in
board_decides: Does the landlord (or a family member, or a purchaser) in good faith need the unit to live in for at least one year?
Was the tenant paid the compensation the Act requires (one month's rent) by the termination date?
Under section 83, whether to delay or refuse the eviction.

items.tab_name: Evidence on the Landlord's Good Faith
items.label: Evidence that questions the landlord's good faith
items.why: The Board looks at whether the landlord genuinely intends to move in. Re-listing the unit, demands for a rent increase or earlier attempts to end the tenancy can cast doubt on that.

examples.excerpt: whether there was good faith at the time the N12 was served. 19.
Landlord has a good faith intention to reside in the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation.

items.label: Whether you received one month's rent as compensation
items.why: An N12 eviction order requires the compensation to have been paid by the termination date.
documents: Bank statement or receipt showing the payment, or its absence

items.label: What you need in order to move
items.why: Members often delay N12 evictions to give a family time to find housing. Explain your situation and bring proof of your housing search.

T2.label: T2 – Tenant's rights (interference, harassment, illegal entry)
board_decides: Did the landlord do what you allege, under section 29 of the Act?
If so, what remedy is fair: rent abatement, out-of-pocket costs, an order to stop, or a fine.

items.label: A dated log of each incident
items.why: T2 applications turn on specific incidents. Members weigh dates, details and whether the record was made at the time.
documents: Timeline with date, time, what happened, who was there

items.label: Messages, notices and letters
items.why: Written communication shows what the landlord said and did, and when.
documents: Notices of entry (or the lack of them)

items.label: What it cost you
items.why: Abatements and costs need a number. Receipts and a short calculation help the member award an amount.
documents: A calculation of the abatement you are asking for

T6.label: T6 – Maintenance and repairs
board_decides: Did the landlord fail to meet maintenance obligations or health, safety and housing standards?
Did the landlord know about the problem, and how long did it last?
What remedy fits: rent abatement, repairs ordered, costs.

items.label: Proof you told the landlord about each problem
items.why: Members look at when the landlord knew. Dated written requests are the clearest proof.
documents: Emails, texts, letters or work-order requests, with dates

items.label: Photos, videos and reports showing the problem
items.why: Dated photos and inspection reports (for example a municipal property standards order) show what the problem was and how long it lasted.

items.label: How much rent abatement you are asking for, and why
items.why: Abatement is usually a share of rent for the period the problem lasted. Show the period, the share you ask for, and any receipts.
documents: Receipts for repairs or replacement items

examples.excerpt: At the hearing, the Tenant indicated he sought only a $2,150.00 abatement in respect of the T6 Application (as opposed to the $5,375.00 abatement in the application).

The Landlord also sought to have the T6 application dismissed as there said the allegations were too vague, did not include specific dates and the Tenant sought a rent abatement under Remedy 9 instead
